newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Pope says Christianity guarantees Czech future.
newsitem.headline: Pope says Christianity guarantees Czech future.

text.p: Pope John Paul celebrated mass with more than 100,000 people on Sunday to mark the millennium of the death of a saint and told Czechs their long Christian tradition was the guarantor of their future.
The 76-year-old Pontiff, on the final day of a weekend visit to the Czech Republic, commemorated the 1,000th anniversary of the martyrdom of St Adalbert with an appeal to Czechs to renew their faith.

"Your Christian history is not over. Your saints are not silent. Your saints are alive. They are the guarantors of your past and of your future," the Pope told the crowd gathered on a blustery overcast day on Prague's Letna Plain.
The Pope, who has suffered a series of health problems in recent years, spoke in a strong voice from the raised altar platform backed by a huge wooden cross and covered in a scaffolding canopy.

Many worshippers, some of whom had come from Poland, Germany and Slovakia, were dressed in overcoats against the cold and carried yellow and white Vatican flags as the Pope said mass with Czech bishops.
Prague Archbishop Cardinal Miloslav Vlk, officiating at the mass, said more than 120,000 were in the crowd.
Security was tight with police on roofs of buildings surrounding Letna, scene of Soviet-era military parades and of huge demonstrations in the 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which toppled communism.
Pope John Paul told the crowd that Adalbert, a Czech bishop who took the gospel to the Pope's native Poland and other parts of central Europe, remained an inspiration today.
"He is a sign of that harmony and cooperation which ought to exist between the church and society. He is a sign of the link between the Czech and Polish nations," he said.

Pope John Paul, on his third trip to Prague since the fall of communism, has used this visit to call for a revival of religion in the country and attack imported Western hedonism in its highly secular society.

Asked if the Pope was resigned to materialism taking root in Eastern Europe, Vatican spokesman Joaquim Navarro- Valls said: "There is the cult of the Mercedes but things are better than they were before."
Relations between the church and the communist authorities in former Czechoslovakia were among the worst in Eastern Europe. Many priests were arrested and much church property was confiscated.
Some tensions remain and the church is still trying to secure the return of property.
Earlier the Pontiff held brief talks with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who told CTK news agency the issue of returning church property confiscated under communism had not been raised.
"He (the Pope) looks at the Czech situation in a historical context and through the eyes of history," Navarro-Valls said, adding that today's problems were not as bad as in Adalberts's day.

Pope John Paul was later due to hold an ecumenical service with other Czech church leaders in Prague's St Vitus Cathedral. The Pope has been eager for Christians of all denominations to be as united in spirit as possible before the start of the third millennium.
